introduction: Every enquiry, site visit, booking and home handover at Tridasa runs on someone's personal data. This playbook explains what India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the DPDP Rules, 2025 expect of us, and what each of us must do differently at work. Read it fully, then take the assessment.

chapters.title: Why this matters to a real-estate company
chapters.content:
A single customer journey at Tridasa Rise touches a lot of personal data: a phone number from a Facebook ad, a name in the Experience Center visitor register, PAN and Aadhaar for the booking, bank and loan details, family members on the sale deed, and CCTV footage at Nallagandla. Channel partners, home-loan banks, CRM and SAP S/4HANA all hold pieces of it.

The DPDP Act makes Tridasa legally accountable for all of it, including what our vendors do on our behalf. Penalties reach ₹250 crore per instance. More importantly, our brand promise is "Brightening Lives": a buyer who trusts us with their family's details expects us to look after them.

The one-line rule

Collect only what you need, use it only for the reason you told the customer, keep it safe, and delete it when the job is done.

chapters.title: Key terms you will hear
chapters.content:
TermMeaningAt Tridasa
Personal dataAny data about an individual who can be identified by or in relation to it. s.2(t)Name, phone, email, PAN, Aadhaar, address, photo, salary, CCTV image, site-visit record.
Data PrincipalThe person the data is about. For a child, includes the parent or lawful guardian; for a person with disability, the lawful guardian. s.2(j)Buyers, co-applicants, leads, visitors, employees, labour, vendor contacts.
Data FiduciaryWhoever decides why and how personal data is processed. s.2(i)Tridasa Realty Ventures Pvt. Ltd.
Data ProcessorProcesses data on behalf of a Fiduciary. s.2(k)CRM vendor, digital marketing agency, payroll provider, cloud host, call centre.
Consent ManagerA Board-registered platform that lets people give, manage, review and withdraw consent. s.2(g), Rule 4Operational from 13 Nov 2026.
Personal data breachAny unauthorised processing, accidental disclosure, loss of access, alteration or destruction that compromises confidentiality, integrity or availability. s.2(u)Buyer list emailed to the wrong person, stolen laptop, ransomware on SAP.
BoardData Protection Board of India, a digital-first regulator that inquires and imposes penalties. s.18Breaches are reported here.

Scope. The Act covers personal data collected digitally, and paper data that is later digitised (for example a visitor register typed into CRM, or a scanned KYC copy). It does not cover data a person uses for purely personal or domestic purposes, or data the individual has deliberately made public. s.3

chapters.title: The seven principles
chapters.content:
1. Lawful, fair and transparent. Process only with valid consent or a legitimate use, and tell people what we do.
  2. Purpose limitation. Use data only for the purpose stated when it was collected.
  3. Data minimisation. Collect only what that purpose needs. A brochure request does not need a PAN.
  4. Accuracy. Keep data complete, correct and consistent, especially before using it in a decision or sharing it. s.8(3)
  5. Storage limitation. Erase data once the purpose is served, unless a law requires us to keep it. s.8(7)
  6. Reasonable security safeguards. Prevent breaches with technical and organisational measures. s.8(5)
  7. Accountability. Tridasa remains responsible even when a vendor does the processing. s.8(1)

chapters.title: Consent and notice
chapters.content:
Consent is valid only if it is free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, given by a clear affirmative action, and limited to the data needed for the stated purpose. s.6(1)

Valid

  • An unticked checkbox the visitor ticks: "Send me updates about Tridasa projects on WhatsApp."
  • Separate checkboxes for project updates and for partner offers.
  • A clear "Unsubscribe" or "Stop" option in every marketing message.

Not valid

  • Pre-ticked boxes, or "by visiting this site you agree".
  • Making a booking conditional on agreeing to marketing by an interior-design partner.
  • Privacy terms buried inside a 30-page sale agreement.

Every request for consent comes with a notice s.5, Rule 3. The notice must stand on its own, be in clear and plain language, and give:

  • an itemised description of the personal data and the specific purpose of processing;
  • how to withdraw consent, as easily as it was given, and how to exercise rights;
  • how to complain to the Data Protection Board.

A customer may ask for the notice in English or any of the 22 languages in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, including Telugu, Hindi and Urdu. For customers whose data we collected before the Act came into force, we must send a notice as soon as reasonably practicable. s.5(2)

Withdrawal. When a customer withdraws consent, stop the processing (and make our vendors stop) within a reasonable time. Withdrawal does not make earlier processing unlawful, and it does not erase records a law requires us to keep, such as sale agreements and tax records. s.6(4)–(6)

chapters.title: Legitimate uses: when consent is not needed
chapters.content:
Section 7 lists situations where we can process data without separate consent. The common ones for us:

Legitimate useTridasa exampleLimit
Data voluntarily given for a specific purpose s.7(a)A visitor emails sales@tridasa.in asking for a brochure and leaves a phone number.Use it to send the brochure and follow up on that enquiry, not to add to unrelated campaigns.
Compliance with law or a court order s.7(d)–(e)Telangana RERA, tax authorities or a court lawfully require buyer details.Share only what is required; route through Legal.
Medical emergency or threat to life s.7(f)Sharing an injured worker's blood group and emergency contact with a hospital.Only what the emergency needs.
Disaster or breakdown of public order s.7(h)Sharing site headcount with rescue teams during a flood.Only for the duration of the event.
Employment purposes s.7(i)Payroll, attendance, PF and ESI filings, preventing corporate espionage.Not for unrelated monitoring or marketing.

chapters.title: Data Principal rights and how we respond
chapters.content:
Access s.11

A summary of their data and our processing, and who we shared it with.

Correction & erasure s.12

Correct, complete, update, or erase data no longer needed (unless law requires us to keep it).

Grievance redressal s.13

A readily available way to complain to us before going to the Board.

Nomination s.14

Name someone to exercise their rights on death or incapacity.

There is no right to data portability under the DPDP Act. Do not promise one.

  1. Don't handle it alone. Any request about a person's own data (whatever words they use) goes to the DPO mailbox the same day.
  2. Verify identity before revealing or changing anything. Never confirm details over an unverified call.
  3. Log it. The DPO records the request, the deadline and every action.
  4. Respond within the published timeline. Rule 14 caps grievance responses at 90 days; Tridasa aims for 30.

chapters.title: Children and persons with disability
chapters.content:
A child is anyone under 18. Before processing a child's data, we need verifiable consent of the parent or lawful guardian, checked against reliable identity and age details (Rule 10). For a person with disability who has a lawful guardian, the guardian gives consent. s.9

Contests like #MYKUTUMBAM

Family photos often include children. Collect verifiable parental consent before using them, and never use a child's data for tracking, behavioural monitoring or targeted advertising. These are prohibited outright. s.9(3)

chapters.title: Retention, accuracy and erasure
chapters.content:
• Leads that never convert: erase once the follow-up purpose is over, or when the person asks or stops engaging, unless a law requires us to keep them.
  • Booking, agreement, payment and tax records: keep for the period the law prescribes (Legal will publish a schedule), then erase.
  • Processing logs and traffic data: keep for at least one year so incidents can be investigated. Rule 6, Rule 8(3)
  • Before sharing data with a bank, RERA or another fiduciary, check it is accurate and complete.
  • When we erase, our processors must erase too.

chapters.title: Security rules for everyone
chapters.content:
Rule 6 requires reasonable safeguards including encryption, obfuscation or masking; access control; logs and monitoring; backups for continuity; and security terms in vendor contracts. For you, that means:

Do

  • Use only Tridasa-approved systems (CRM, SAP, official email) for customer data.
  • Lock your screen; use strong, unique passwords and MFA.
  • Share files with named people, with access that expires.
  • Lock away printed KYC and shred it when done.
  • Report lost devices immediately.

Don't

  • Forward customer lists to personal Gmail or WhatsApp.
  • Share logins, even within a team.
  • Leave booking files on the Experience Center desk.
  • Download full CRM exports "just in case".
  • Paste customer data into unapproved apps or AI tools.

chapters.title: Breach response
chapters.content:
If you suspect a breach, report it the moment you notice. You will not be blamed for reporting; you can be for hiding it.

  1. Report to the DPO and IT (incident channel) immediately. Do not delete emails, wipe devices or "clean up" evidence.
  2. Contain: IT revokes access, recalls emails, isolates systems.
  3. Notify without delay: the DPO informs the Data Protection Board and each affected person, in plain language, with what happened, likely consequences and steps they can take. s.8(6), Rule 7
  4. Within 72 hours of becoming aware, a detailed report goes to the Board: facts, cause, mitigation, and who caused it if known.
  5. Learn: the root cause is fixed and recorded.

chapters.title: Vendors, channel partners and cross-border transfer
chapters.content:
• Engage a Data Processor only under a valid written contract. Tridasa stays responsible for what they do. s.8(2)
  • When a contract ends or consent is withdrawn, make sure the vendor erases our data.
  • Personal data may go abroad (for example a cloud server) except to countries the Central Government restricts by notification. Check with the DPO before using any new overseas tool. s.16
  • Channel partners sharing leads with us must confirm the lead consented to being contacted by Tridasa.

chapters.title: Penalties
chapters.content:
Breach of dutyMaximum penalty
Failure to take reasonable security safeguards to prevent a breach₹250 crore
Failure to notify the Board or affected people of a breach₹200 crore
Breach of obligations about children's data₹200 crore
Breach of additional duties of a Significant Data Fiduciary₹150 crore
Breach of any other provision of the Act or Rules₹50 crore
Data Principal's breach of their duties (s.15), such as false complaints or impersonation₹10,000

The Board can inquire, impose penalties and accept voluntary undertakings. Appeals go to the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT) within 60 days. s.29, s.33, Schedule

chapters.title: Desk rules by team
chapters.content:
Sales & Experience Center

  • Collect only name, contact and requirement at the first visit.
  • Keep the visitor register face-down; don't photograph it.
  • Display the CCTV notice at the entrance.

Marketing

  • Unticked, separate consent boxes on every form.
  • Honour "stop" within a reasonable time across all agencies.
  • Parental consent for any child's photo.

CRM, Legal & Finance

  • Store KYC only in CRM or SAP, never on desktops.
  • Share loan files with banks over approved channels only.
  • Follow the retention schedule.

HR & Projects

  • Restrict access to salary, health and ID records.
  • Labour data only for attendance, wages, safety and legal filings.
  • Delete unsuccessful candidates' CVs on schedule.

This playbook summarises the DPDP Act, 2023 and DPDP Rules, 2025 for internal training. It is not legal advice; Tridasa's DPO and legal counsel decide specific cases.

questions.question: Tridasa decides why and how buyers' personal data is processed for bookings. Under the DPDP Act, Tridasa is a:
options: Data Fiduciary
Data Processor
Data Principal
Consent Manager
questions.explanation: The entity that determines the purpose and means of processing is the Data Fiduciary (s.2(i)). Our CRM vendor would be a Data Processor.

questions.question: Which of these falls OUTSIDE the DPDP Act?
options: Contacts a person keeps on their own phone for purely personal or domestic use
Scanned KYC copies of a flat buyer
Experience Center visitor details later typed into the CRM
Employee payroll records in HRMS
questions.explanation: Section 3 excludes data processed by an individual for a personal or domestic purpose. Paper data that is digitised later is covered.

questions.question: A home buyer's name, PAN and phone number are all examples of:
options: Personal data, because the buyer can be identified from them
Sensitive personal data, a separate category under the DPDP Act
Public data, because PAN is issued by the government
Non-personal data once stored in SAP
questions.explanation: Personal data is any data about an identifiable individual (s.2(t)). The DPDP Act has no separate 'sensitive' category.

questions.question: By when must the DPDP Act's core obligations (notice, security safeguards, breach reporting, rights) be fully in place?
options: 13 November 2025
1 January 2026
There is no deadline; compliance is voluntary
questions.explanation: The Rules were notified on 13 Nov 2025 with an 18-month runway; the substantive obligations commence on 13 May 2027.

questions.question: Which describes valid consent under the DPDP Act?
options: Free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, given by a clear affirmative action
Assumed when a visitor browses tridasa.in for more than a minute
Given through a pre-ticked box the visitor did not untick
Valid for any purpose once given for one purpose
questions.explanation: Section 6(1) sets these conditions and requires a clear affirmative action.

questions.question: Our enquiry form has a pre-ticked box: 'I agree to receive offers from Tridasa and its partners'. What should we do?
options: Replace it with an unticked box the person must tick, kept separate from the enquiry itself
Keep it, since the person can untick it if they object
Keep it, but add the clause to the website footer
Remove the box and treat every enquiry as consent for partner offers
questions.explanation: A pre-ticked box is not a clear affirmative action. Marketing consent must be separate and actively given.

questions.question: A buyer messages 'STOP' to our WhatsApp marketing updates. What is the correct response?
options: Stop marketing messages within a reasonable time and make sure our agencies stop too
Ask the buyer to send a signed letter to withdraw
Continue until the current campaign ends
Delete the buyer's entire booking file, including the sale agreement
questions.explanation: Withdrawal must be as easy as giving consent (s.6(4)). Records required by law, like the sale agreement, are retained.

questions.question: Can we make a flat booking conditional on the buyer agreeing to share data with an interior-design partner for marketing?
options: No. Consent must be limited to data necessary for the specified purpose and cannot be bundled
Yes, if it is mentioned in the booking form
Yes, because the partner may offer the buyer a discount
Only for buyers paying in cash
questions.explanation: Section 6(1) limits consent to what is necessary for the specified purpose; unrelated purposes cannot be forced.

questions.question: What must a privacy notice given with a consent request contain?
options: The personal data and purpose, how to withdraw consent and exercise rights, and how to complain to the Board
Only a link to the company's annual report
The names of every employee who can access the data
Only the company's GST number and address
questions.explanation: Section 5 and Rule 3 require an itemised description of data and purposes, the way to withdraw and exercise rights, and how to complain to the Board.

questions.question: A Telugu-speaking buyer asks for our privacy notice in Telugu. What applies?
options: They can access the notice in English or any of the 22 Eighth Schedule languages, including Telugu
Notices are only available in English
Only Hindi and English are permitted
We can refuse because the sale agreement is in English
questions.explanation: Section 5(3) gives the option to access the notice in English or any Eighth Schedule language.

questions.question: Is it enough to include our privacy terms on page 27 of the sale agreement?
options: No. The notice should be presented independently, in clear and plain language
Yes, as long as the buyer signs every page
Yes, if the font size is at least 8 points
Yes, notices are optional for existing customers
questions.explanation: Rule 3 requires a notice that is understandable on its own, without reference to other information, in clear and plain language.

questions.question: For customers who booked in 2024, before the Act took effect, what does Tridasa owe them?
options: A notice about their data and rights as soon as reasonably practicable
Nothing, since the Act is not retrospective in any way
Immediate deletion of all their data
A fresh sale agreement
questions.explanation: Section 5(2) requires notice for consent given before commencement as soon as reasonably practicable.

questions.question: A visitor emails sales@tridasa.in for a brochure and includes a phone number. What can we do without separate consent?
options: Send the brochure and follow up on that enquiry
Add the number to every future campaign, including partner offers
Share the number with channel partners
Sell the lead to a home-loan aggregator
questions.explanation: Data given voluntarily for a specified purpose may be used for that purpose (s.7(a)), but not for unrelated ones.

questions.question: Processing employees' attendance and bank details for payroll is:
options: A legitimate use for employment purposes under s.7(i)
Allowed only with fresh consent every month
Prohibited under the DPDP Act
Allowed only for employees above a certain grade
questions.explanation: Section 7(i) permits processing for employment purposes.

questions.question: A worker is injured at the Tridasa Rise site. Can we share his blood group and emergency contact with the hospital?
options: Yes, responding to a medical emergency is a legitimate use
No, written consent is always required first
Only after the DPO approves in writing
Only if he is a permanent employee
questions.explanation: Section 7(f) covers responding to a medical emergency involving a threat to life or health.

questions.question: Telangana RERA lawfully requires details of allottees in a project. What is right?
options: Share what the law requires, through Legal, as a legitimate use
Refuse unless every buyer consents individually
Share the full CRM export to be safe
Ask the authority to buy the data
questions.explanation: Processing to comply with a law or order is a legitimate use (s.7). Share only what is required.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a right under the DPDP Act?
options: Data portability
Access to a summary of personal data
Correction and erasure
Nominating someone to exercise rights after death or incapacity
questions.explanation: The Act gives access (s.11), correction and erasure (s.12), grievance redressal (s.13) and nomination (s.14). It has no portability right.

questions.question: A buyer calls the front desk asking what personal data Tridasa holds about her. What should you do?
options: Route it to the DPO the same day; identity is verified before anything is shared
Read out her details over the phone right away
Tell her the law does not allow such requests
Ask her to file an RTI application
questions.explanation: Access requests (s.11) are handled centrally with identity verification and a logged response.

questions.question: Under the DPDP Rules, what is the maximum time to respond to a Data Principal's grievance?
options: 90 days
7 years
24 hours
There is no time limit
questions.explanation: Rule 14 requires a published response period not exceeding 90 days. Tridasa aims for 30.

questions.question: A buyer wants her son to be able to exercise her data rights if she dies or becomes incapacitated. This is the right to:
options: Nominate
Data portability
Be forgotten by the Board
Appeal to TDSAT
questions.explanation: Section 14 gives every Data Principal the right to nominate another individual.

questions.question: A lead visited the Experience Center 2 years ago, never booked, and has not responded since. What should happen to their data?
options: Erase it, since the purpose is no longer served and no law requires us to keep it
Keep it forever in case they buy later
Move it to a personal laptop for safekeeping
Sell it to another developer
questions.explanation: Section 8(7) requires erasure once the specified purpose is no longer being served, unless retention is required by law.

questions.question: For how long must logs of personal data processing be kept, at minimum, under the Rules?
options: One year
One week
Ten years in every case
They must not be kept at all
questions.explanation: Rule 6 and Rule 8(3) require logs and traffic data to be retained for at least one year.

questions.question: Marketing wants to use Experience Center visitor numbers to sell a partner's insurance products. Is this allowed?
options: No, not without fresh consent for that purpose
Yes, visitors already gave their numbers
Yes, if the calls are made after 6 pm
Yes, if the partner pays a fee
questions.explanation: Purpose limitation: data collected for a site visit cannot be reused for an unrelated purpose without consent.

questions.question: Before sending a buyer's details to her home-loan bank, what must we ensure?
options: The data is complete, accurate and consistent
The bank pays for the data
The buyer's file is printed in colour
Nothing; the bank will verify it
questions.explanation: Section 8(3) requires accuracy when data is used in a decision or disclosed to another Data Fiduciary.

questions.question: After a personal data breach, what must Tridasa do?
options: Inform the Board and each affected person without delay, and send the Board a detailed report within 72 hours
Inform no one if the data was recovered
Inform the Board within 1 year
Post about it on social media only
questions.explanation: Section 8(6) and Rule 7: intimation without delay, and a detailed report to the Board within 72 hours.

questions.question: You emailed a list of 40 buyers to the wrong external address. What do you do first?
options: Report it immediately to the DPO and IT incident channel
Delete the sent email and say nothing
Ask the recipient informally to ignore it and close the matter
Wait to see if any buyer complains
questions.explanation: Speed matters for the 72-hour clock. Report first; don't destroy evidence.

questions.question: Which of these is one of the 'reasonable security safeguards' listed in Rule 6?
options: Encryption, masking or obfuscation of personal data
Sharing one CRM login across the sales team
Keeping all KYC copies on desktops for quick access
Disabling access logs to save storage
questions.explanation: Rule 6 lists encryption or masking, access control, logs and monitoring, backups, and contractual safeguards.

questions.question: You want to finish a booking report at home. How should you move the customer data?
options: Use only Tridasa-approved systems and devices
Forward it to your personal Gmail
Send it to yourself on WhatsApp
Copy it to a personal USB drive
questions.explanation: Personal accounts and devices sit outside our safeguards and logs.

questions.question: Under the DPDP Act, a 'child' is anyone under:
options: 18 years
13 years
16 years
21 years
questions.explanation: Section 2(f) defines a child as an individual who has not completed eighteen years.

questions.question: The #MYKUTUMBAM contest receives a family photo that includes two children. What do we need before using it?
options: Verifiable consent from the parent or lawful guardian
Nothing; the photo was sent voluntarily
The children's own verbal consent
Only a watermark on the photo
questions.explanation: Section 9(1) and Rule 10 require verifiable parental consent for children's data.

questions.question: Which processing of children's data is prohibited outright?
options: Tracking, behavioural monitoring or targeted advertising directed at children
Storing a child's name as a nominee with parental consent
Recording a child's name as a family member on an allotment letter
Responding to a parent's query
questions.explanation: Section 9(3) prohibits tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children.

questions.question: A buyer is a person with disability who has a court-appointed lawful guardian. Whose consent do we take?
options: The lawful guardian's
Any relative present at the site
The channel partner's
No consent is needed
questions.explanation: Section 9(1) requires verifiable consent of the lawful guardian.

questions.question: Tridasa hires a digital marketing agency to run lead campaigns. Which is true?
options: Engage them only under a valid contract; Tridasa stays responsible for their processing
Responsibility moves fully to the agency
No contract is needed if the agency is reputable
The agency can reuse the leads for its other clients
questions.explanation: Section 8(1)-(2): the Fiduciary remains responsible and may engage a Processor only under a valid contract.

questions.question: Can Tridasa store customer data on a cloud server outside India?
options: Yes, except in countries the Central Government restricts by notification
Never, under any circumstances
Only in countries that share a border with India
Only if every customer signs a separate form
questions.explanation: Section 16 allows transfers except to countries restricted by notification.

questions.question: What is a Consent Manager under the DPDP framework?
options: A Board-registered platform that lets people give, manage, review and withdraw consent
The sales manager who collects consent forms
Any vendor that stores consent records
A government officer who approves each consent
questions.explanation: Section 2(g) and Rule 4. Consent Managers can operate from 13 November 2026.

questions.question: Our contract with a call-centre vendor ends. What should happen to the lead data they hold?
options: Ensure the vendor erases it
Let the vendor keep it for future business
Ask them to sell it back to us
Nothing; it is their data now
questions.explanation: Section 8(7)(b) requires the Fiduciary to cause its Processors to erase data that is no longer needed.

questions.question: Maximum penalty for failing to take reasonable security safeguards to prevent a breach:
options: ₹250 crore
₹5 crore
₹1,000 crore
questions.explanation: Schedule to the Act, item 1.

questions.question: Maximum penalty for failing to notify the Board and affected people of a breach:
options: ₹200 crore
₹50 lakh
₹10 crore
No penalty
questions.explanation: Schedule to the Act, item 2.

questions.question: Which is a duty of the Data Principal under s.15, with a penalty of up to ₹10,000?
options: Not filing a false or frivolous grievance or complaint
Reading every privacy notice twice
Paying a fee to exercise rights
Visiting the Experience Center in person
questions.explanation: Section 15 duties include not impersonating others, not suppressing information and not filing false or frivolous complaints.

questions.question: An order of the Data Protection Board can be appealed to:
options: TDSAT, within 60 days
Telangana RERA, within 1 year
The local police station
No one; Board orders are final
questions.explanation: Section 29: appeals lie to the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal within 60 days.
